---
title: "The exponential family"
---

The [generalized-linear-model page](generalized-linear-models.qmd) stated that a standard generalized linear model uses an exponential-family response. We now define that family. Normal, Bernoulli, and Poisson distributions look different, but they can all be written in a common form.

The exponential-family form lets us separate the observed response, a transformed parameter,
and any dispersion term. This representation does not make the distributions identical. It shows which
mathematical roles they share.

## The common form

A distribution belongs to the [**exponential family**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=214) if its density or mass function can be written as

$$
p(y\mid\theta,\phi)
=
\exp\left(
\frac{y\theta-b(\theta)}{a(\phi)}+c(y,\phi)
\right).
$$

The symbols have specific jobs:

1. $y$ is the observed response.
2. $\theta$ is the natural parameter.
3. $\phi$ is a dispersion parameter when the family has one.
4. $b(\theta)$ determines the mean and variance.
5. $c(y,\phi)$ contains terms that do not involve $\theta$.

This notation is abstract because it must cover several distributions. We will make it concrete with the Bernoulli distribution.

The natural parameter $\theta$ need not equal a familiar mean parameter. It is
the parameter value that makes the observed response enter linearly in the
exponent. The function $b(\theta)$ then provides the normalization needed for
the probabilities or density to sum or integrate to one.

## Rewrite the Bernoulli distribution

For $y\in\{0,1\}$,

$$
p(y\mid\pi)=\pi^y(1-\pi)^{1-y}.
$$

Taking logs gives

$$
\log p(y\mid\pi)
=
y\log\pi+(1-y)\log(1-\pi).
$$

Collect the terms involving $y$:

$$
\log p(y\mid\pi)
=
y\log\frac{\pi}{1-\pi}+\log(1-\pi).
$$

Thus the natural parameter is

$$
\theta=\log\frac{\pi}{1-\pi},
$$

which is the log odds. The Bernoulli canonical link will arise from this same quantity.

To identify the remaining pieces, solve for $\pi$ in terms of $\theta$:

$$
\pi=\frac{e^\theta}{1+e^\theta}.
$$

Then

$$
\log(1-\pi)=-\log(1+e^\theta),
$$

so

$$
\log p(y\mid\theta)
=y\theta-\log(1+e^\theta).
$$

For the Bernoulli family,

$$
b(\theta)=\log(1+e^\theta),
$$

there is no separately estimated dispersion parameter, and $c(y)=0$ under this
representation.

## Why this family is useful

For this form,

$$
\mathbb{E}[Y]=b'(\theta)
$$

and

$$
\mathrm{Var}(Y)=a(\phi)b''(\theta).
$$

The conditional variance is thus tied to the conditional mean in a family-specific way. The function that expresses this relation is the [**variance function**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=214). Bernoulli variance is $\pi(1-\pi)$. Poisson variance is $\lambda$. Normal variance is governed by a separate dispersion parameter.

For the Bernoulli form,

$$
b'(\theta)
=\frac{e^\theta}{1+e^\theta}
=\pi.
$$

The first derivative recovers the mean. The second derivative is

$$
b''(\theta)
=\frac{e^\theta}{(1+e^\theta)^2}
=\pi(1-\pi),
$$

which recovers the variance. The mean-variance relation is thus encoded in the
same $b$ function.

This relation is one reason the response distribution matters. Choosing a family is not merely choosing the range of possible outcomes. It also chooses a mean variance relation.

## Write the Poisson exponential-family form

For count $y\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$,

$$
p(y\mid\lambda)
=\frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^y}{y!}.
$$

Taking logs gives

$$
\log p(y\mid\lambda)
=y\log\lambda-\lambda-\log(y!).
$$

Set

$$
\theta=\log\lambda.
$$

Since $\lambda=e^\theta$, the log mass becomes

$$
\log p(y\mid\theta)
=y\theta-e^\theta-\log(y!).
$$

Thus

$$
b(\theta)=e^\theta
$$

and

$$
c(y)=-\log(y!).
$$

Both the first and second derivatives of $b(\theta)$ equal $e^\theta=\lambda$.
This yields the Poisson equality of mean and variance.

## Connect natural parameters to canonical links

A [**canonical link**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=214) sets the linear predictor equal to the natural parameter.
For the Bernoulli family,

$$
\eta=\theta=\log\frac{\pi}{1-\pi},
$$

so the canonical link is the logit. For the Poisson family,

$$
\eta=\theta=\log\lambda,
$$

so the canonical link is the log link.

Canonical links make the predictor enter the exponential-family form through its natural parameter.
They are not required by the response support. Another monotone link can map to
the same allowed mean range while producing a noncanonical model.

Not every generalized linear model must use its canonical link. Canonical links often simplify
estimation and interpretation, but the model choice remains separate.

## The family does not include every useful distribution

The negative binomial is often represented in an exponential family form under a fixed dispersion parameter, but regression practice usually estimates that dispersion. Mixtures, zero inflated models, and ordered beta models require additional structure. Thus, generalized linear modeling provides a useful architecture, not a catalog of every model linguists may need.

Membership in the exponential family also does not establish that a family is adequate for a
particular response. A Poisson likelihood has count support, but a linguistic
count can still have more variation than its mean. Mathematical convenience
does not replace measurement and predictive checks.

## Verify the derivatives numerically

At $\theta=0$, the Bernoulli mean is $.5$ and variance is $.25$. At
$\theta=\log4$, the mean is $.8$ and variance is $.16$:

```{r}
#| label: verify-exponential-family-derivatives
#| echo: true
theta <- c(0, log(4))
bernoulli_mean <- exp(theta) / (1 + exp(theta))
bernoulli_variance <- bernoulli_mean * (1 - bernoulli_mean)

data.frame(
  theta = theta,
  mean = bernoulli_mean,
  variance = bernoulli_variance
)
```

This calculation makes the mean-variance coupling concrete before any
regression predictors are added.
